lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eCon \u003cb\u003eCO₂\:
"

With CO₂ (dry ice) a carboxylate forms and, on acidifying, a carboxylic acid with one more carbon than the starting halide. With an ester the first equivalent gives a ketone (after expelling the alkoxide), but this is more reactive than the ester and reacts with a second equivalent: a tertiary alcohol with two identical R groups is obtained.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eCuanto más electropos:
"

The more electropositive the metal, the more ionic the C–M bond and the more reactive and basic the carbanion: R–Li > R–MgX > R–ZnX > R₂CuLi. Organolithiums react similarly to Grignards (sometimes faster); Gilman cuprates (R₂CuLi) are milder: they substitute halides and add 1,4 to enones without attacking the carbonyl.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eEl \u003cb\u003ereact:
"

The Grignard reagent is prepared by adding an alkyl or aryl halide to metallic magnesium in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF), which solvates the Mg. The carbon, formerly electrophilic (δ+ in C–Br), becomes nucleophilic and basic (δ− in C–Mg): there is a polarity inversion (umpolung). Everything must be anhydrous: water destroys it.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eEl carbono del Grigna:
"

The Grignard carbon is the conjugate base of an alkane (pKa ≈ 50): it deprotonates any acidic H (H₂O, ROH, RCOOH, RNH₂, R–C≡C–H) and becomes the alkane R–H, losing its usefulness. That is why you must work with dry material and protect the OH or NH groups of the substrates. Turn on “Presence of water” to see it.

"
lit.\u0027\u003cp\u003eEl carbono nucleófilo:
"

The nucleophilic carbon attacks the carbonyl carbon and a magnesium alkoxide forms; then the acid work-up (H₃O⁺) protonates it. A C–C bond is thus formed: formaldehyde → primary alcohol, aldehydes → secondary, ketones → tertiary. Choose R and the electrophile and move the progress control.

"
